unit.perspectives_title: Whose Government? Perspectives on Power in Tennessee
unit.perspectives_intro: This section traces how power is arranged and shared across Tennessee government — divided among three branches, balanced across three regions, and layered from the state down to your own county and city. It is Government Hack–authored instructional synthesis grounded in this unit's sourced record — not a primary source.
perspectives: Tennessee splits authority into three departments — legislative, executive, and judicial — the same design as the national government, applied to the state (GC.28).
East, Middle, and West Tennessee each carry distinct histories and interests; the state deliberately balances offices and representation across all three (GC.28).
Authority flows from the state down to counties, cities, and consolidated metropolitan governments — each one created by, and answerable to, the state (GC.29).
Government reaches all the way down to your own district and your own officials — and this unit asks you to identify them, contact them, and take part (GC.30).
unit.tn_connection: This whole unit is the Tennessee Connection. Foundations traced government in the abstract; here it becomes concrete and local — the Capitol in Nashville, the three Grand Divisions marked by the three stars on the state flag, the ninety-five counties on the state map, and the specific legislators elected from your own district. Tennessee is not an example in this unit; Tennessee is the subject (GC.28–GC.30).
unit.tn_connection_task: Tennessee is the classroom for this entire unit. Choose one and record it with a source: (a) name the three Grand Divisions and explain what the flag's three stars stand for; (b) identify which local-government model runs your own county; or (c) look up and record your current governor and your two state legislators from an official Tennessee source.

engagement: 7.2 relevance (your county, your legislators, your courts)

unit.belief_check: Predict first: Which level of government — your city, your county, or the state — do you think has the biggest effect on your daily life? Write your gut answer now; you'll test it against how Tennessee actually divides and shares power.

play.name: Who Governs? / Which Court?
play.how: 4-minute game (GC.28–GC.29). Read a one-line scenario — a felony trial, a property-line dispute, a new city zoning rule, a statewide budget — and call which trial court (Circuit, Chancery, or Criminal) or which level of government (city, county, or state) handles it. Students feel how Tennessee's three branches and its layers of local government split the work.

GC.28.title: Tennessee's Three Branches
GC.28.tn: Identify the functions of departments and agencies of the executive, legislative, and judicial branches in the state of Tennessee.
GC.28.ican: I can identify the functions of the departments and agencies of Tennessee's executive, legislative, and judicial branches.

vocab.def: The three legal regions of Tennessee — East, Middle, and West — recognized in state law and marked by the three stars on the state flag; the state balances offices and representation across all three.

A part-time lawmaking body whose members keep regular jobs at home and meet for a limited number of 'legislative days'; Tennessee's General Assembly is designed this way, unlike the full-time U.S. Congress.

Tennessee's method for selecting appellate judges: the governor appoints them, and they then face yes-or-no 'retention' elections rather than contested partisan races — a merit-based approach that shapes the state court system.

sources.title: Tennessee Constitution, Article II, Section 1
sources.quote: The powers of the Government shall be divided into three distinct departments: Legislative, Executive, and Judicial.
sources.repo: Constitution of the State of Tennessee

sources.title: Tennessee Constitution, Article VI, Section 1
sources.quote: The judicial power of this State shall be vested in one Supreme Court and in such Circuit, Chancery and other inferior Courts as the Legislature shall from time to time, ordain and establish; in the Judges thereof, and in Justices of the Peace.
sources.repo: Constitution of the State of Tennessee

cfu.stem: In Tennessee's trial-court system, which court is a court of equity, presided over by a Chancellor?
cfu.why: DOK 2: Chancery courts are Tennessee's courts of equity — handling matters such as contracts, property disputes, and injunctions — and are led by a Chancellor. Circuit courts hear general civil and criminal trials; Criminal courts handle felonies in the larger judicial districts.

auth.close: Tennessee's government is built on the same three-branch design as the national government: the state constitution divides power into 'three distinct departments: Legislative, Executive, and Judicial.' The executive branch — led by the governor — runs the departments and agencies that carry out state law, from Education and Health to Safety and Transportation. The legislative branch is the General Assembly, a part-time 'citizen legislature' whose members hold regular jobs back home and meet for only a limited number of 'legislative days,' unlike the year-round Congress. To keep the state balanced, offices and representation are spread across Tennessee's three Grand Divisions — East, Middle, and West — the three stars on the state flag. The judicial branch is a layered court system: Circuit courts hear general civil and criminal trials, Chancery courts (led by Chancellors) decide matters of equity, and Criminal courts handle felonies in the larger districts, all beneath one Supreme Court. Tennessee's appellate judges reach the bench through the 'Tennessee Plan' — appointed, then facing yes-or-no retention elections. (Who is the current Chief Justice of the Tennessee Supreme Court? Look it up from an official source such as tncourts.gov — the five justices choose one of themselves, and it rotates.)
tdq: What does it mean that Tennessee's General Assembly is a part-time 'citizen legislature' with limited legislative days?
How do Chancery, Circuit, and Criminal courts differ in what each one handles?
What is the 'Tennessee Plan,' and how do appellate judges reach the bench under it?

GC.29.title: Local Government in Tennessee
GC.29.tn: Explain the differences among the types of local governments in Tennessee, including county, city, and metro governments, as well as the legal, fiscal, and operational relationships between them and the state government.
GC.29.ican: I can explain the differences among county, city, and metropolitan governments in Tennessee and how they relate legally, fiscally, and operationally to the state.

vocab.def: A system in which a central government — here, the state — holds the primary authority and creates the local governments beneath it, which exercise only the powers the state grants. Tennessee is a unitary state.
The legal principle that a local government has only the powers the state expressly gives it — the reason a Tennessee county or city cannot act beyond what state law allows.

A consolidated government that merges a city and its county into a single unit, authorized by the Tennessee Constitution and approved by local voters — one of the state's structural models alongside county and city governments.

sources.title: Tennessee Constitution, Article VII, Section 1
sources.quote: The qualified voters of each county shall elect for terms of four years a legislative body, a county executive, a Sheriff, a Trustee, a Register, a County Clerk and an Assessor of Property.
sources.repo: Constitution of the State of Tennessee

sources.title: Tennessee Constitution, Article XI, Section 9
sources.quote: The General Assembly may provide for the consolidation of any or all of the governmental and corporate functions now or hereafter vested in municipal corporations with the governmental and corporate functions now or hereafter vested in the counties in which such municipal corporations are located.
sources.repo: Constitution of the State of Tennessee

cfu.stem: Tennessee is a unitary state. What does that mean for your county and city governments?

options.A: They are completely independent of the state
options.B: They report directly to the federal government
options.C: They are created by the state and hold only the powers the state grants them
options.D: They may set aside state law within their own borders

cfu.why: DOK 2: In a unitary system, local governments are 'creatures of the state.' Under Dillon's Rule, Tennessee's counties and cities derive their authority from the state and may exercise only the powers the state grants them.

auth.close: Local government in Tennessee exists only because the state creates it. Tennessee is a unitary state: the state holds the primary authority and hands specific powers down to local governments, which — under 'Dillon's Rule' — may do only what state law allows. Within that system, Tennesseans are governed by several types of local government. Every part of the state lies inside one of its counties, and the voters of each county elect 'a legislative body, a county executive, a Sheriff, a Trustee, a Register, a County Clerk and an Assessor of Property.' Cities (municipalities) form to provide closer services — police, water, zoning — and use different structural models, such as a mayor-council form or a city-commission form. The state constitution also lets voters merge a city and its surrounding county into a single consolidated 'metropolitan' government. Legally, fiscally, and operationally these governments answer to the state: they are chartered under state law, may raise revenue only through taxes the state authorizes, and run programs the state funds and regulates. Look at your own county and city: which model does each use, and which services does each provide?
tdq: What does it mean that Tennessee is a 'unitary' state, and how does Dillon's Rule limit local governments?
How do county, city, and metropolitan governments differ in structure and in the services they provide?
Name the legal, fiscal, and operational ways your local governments depend on the state.

GC.30.title: Identify Your Current Officials
GC.30.tn: Identify the current governor of Tennessee and the representatives in the General Assembly (for a student's respective district). (P, T)
GC.30.ican: I can identify the current governor of Tennessee and the state legislators who represent me, using official sources.

vocab.def: Tennessee's chief executive, elected statewide to a four-year term, who carries out state law, proposes the state budget, and sets policy priorities. Identify the current officeholder from an official source — it changes with elections.

Tennessee's state legislature, made up of a 33-member Senate and a 99-member House of Representatives, which writes and passes state law. These numbers stay the same regardless of who currently serves.
A person a legislator represents. You are a constituent of exactly one state senator and one state representative, determined by the district where you live.

sources.title: Tennessee Constitution, Article III, Section 1
sources.quote: The Supreme Executive power of this State shall be vested in a Governor.
sources.repo: Constitution of the State of Tennessee

sources.title: Tennessee Constitution, Article II, Section 3
sources.quote: The legislative authority of this state shall be vested in a General Assembly, which shall consist of a Senate and House of Representatives, both dependent on the people.
sources.repo: Constitution of the State of Tennessee

cfu.stem: To find out who currently represents you in the Tennessee General Assembly, the best source is —

options.A: the official 'Find My Legislator' tool on the Tennessee General Assembly site (capitol.tn.gov)
options.B: a rumor you saw on social media
options.C: a textbook printed several years ago

cfu.why: DOK 1: Officeholders change with each election, so the accurate way to identify your current senator and representative is the official 'Find My Legislator' address-lookup tool at capitol.tn.gov — not memory, rumor, or an out-of-date book.

auth.close: This standard is a civic-action task: identify the officials who represent you right now. Start with the executive — 'The Supreme Executive power of this State shall be vested in a Governor,' elected statewide to a four-year term. From an official source such as tn.gov, find the current governor's name and the priorities he or she has publicly stated (often in the annual State of the State address or the proposed budget). Next, the legislature: 'The legislative authority of this state shall be vested in a General Assembly, which shall consist of a Senate and House of Representatives.' Tennessee's Senate has 33 members and its House has 99. Every Tennessean lives in exactly one state Senate district and one state House district and is represented by one senator and one representative. Using your home address and the official Tennessee General Assembly 'Find My Legislator' tool at capitol.tn.gov, record your Senate district number, your House district number, and the names of the two people who currently hold those seats. Because officials change with every election, always confirm names, priorities, and districts from the official source — never from memory or from an old book.
tdq: Which official source would you use to find the current governor and his or her stated priorities?
How many members serve in the Tennessee Senate and House, and how is each Tennessean represented in them?
